mcpConnect.introTab: Import this endpoint to drive only this tab’s tools from your assistant — a scoped view of the OS MCP. Every call runs under your identity through the same governed path as the UI (OPA policy, audit, role gates); tools are scoped to your role. For the whole OS, use the MCP button in the top bar of any page.
mcpConnect.introOs: Import this one authenticated endpoint once and drive the whole OS — create → build → preview → deploy, query the marts, score models — from your assistant. Every call runs under your identity through the same governed path as the UI (OPA policy, audit, role gates). Your tools are scoped to your role.
mcpConnect.step1Title: 1 · Your connection (works with any AI platform)
mcpConnect.step1Body: Every AI platform connects the same way: it needs your endpoint URL, and a way to prove it’s you — either managed sign-in (the platform sends you to this OS to log in; nothing to copy) or your personal token (for platforms that use access-token auth). Both connect as {name} ({role}) — same identity, same governance.
mcpConnect.endpointLabel: Endpoint URL — every platform needs this
mcpConnect.tokenLabel: Personal token — for token-based platforms (e.g. Codex, ChatGPT) · treat like a password
mcpConnect.claudeS2: Paste the endpoint URL. Leave everything else empty.
mcpConnect.claudeS3: Choose Managed Authorization (Verwaltete Autorisierung) — no token needed.
mcpConnect.claudeS4: A sign-in window from this OS opens. Sign in with your OS account: username {id}, your usual OS password.
mcpConnect.claudeS5: Click Approve. Done — revocable any time from this OS.
mcpConnect.fallbackTitle: Config-file fallback — only for older Claude Desktop versions without custom connectors
mcpConnect.configBody: Add to <mono>{file}</mono> (Settings → Developer → Edit Config), then restart Claude.
mcpConnect.codexIntro: The richest way to drive the OS from the OpenAI ecosystem — every governed tool, from your terminal. Verified with the Codex desktop app on macOS.
mcpConnect.codexS1: Copy your endpoint URL and personal token above — never paste the token into a Codex chat.
mcpConnect.codexS2: In Terminal, make the token available to Codex (keep the single quotes):
mcpConnect.codexS4: Fully quit Codex (⌘Q) and reopen it — required so Codex picks up the token. Then run {cmd} in a new conversation to confirm {server} is active.
mcpConnect.verify: Verify from Terminal — run {cmd}. The result should show enabled: true, transport: streamable_http, your endpoint URL, and bearer_token_env_var: {envVar}.
mcpConnect.test: Test it — in a new Codex conversation: “Use Sovereign Agentic OS to identify me and list the capabilities available to my account.” Codex returns your delegated identity, role, domains, and tools.
mcpConnect.updating: Updating the token — re-run the {cmd} command with the new token, then fully quit and reopen Codex.
mcpConnect.afterRestart: After restarting your Mac — macOS may clear the launchctl variable. If Codex reports an auth error, re-run step 2 and restart Codex.
mcpConnect.troubleshooting: Troubleshooting — if it was added incorrectly, remove it with {removeCmd} and repeat the steps. On Unauthorized / HTTP 401: confirm the token is valid, wrapped in single quotes, and the variable is named exactly {envVar}; then quit and reopen Codex. Do not use {loginCmd} — the OS uses the personal bearer-token setup above.
mcpConnect.security: Security: typing the token in Terminal may store it in your shell history — clear that entry afterward, or use your organisation’s approved secret manager.
mcpConnect.chatgptS2: Click Add custom connector and give it a name (e.g. “Sovereign OS”).
mcpConnect.chatgptS3: Paste the endpoint URL as the MCP Server URL.
mcpConnect.chatgptS4: Authentication → Access token / API key → paste your personal token from above.
mcpConnect.chatgptS5: Save, then enable it in the chat composer’s tools. ChatGPT now works as you, fully governed.
mcpConnect.step5Body: One command — paste into your terminal:

tokens.title: Access tokens
tokens.intro: A personal access token is how your git client proves it is you. Use it as the password for git clone, git fetch and git push against {path}; any username works. It is stored hashed, shown once, and acts with exactly your own role and domains — never more. A read-only token cannot push; a token narrowed to some repositories cannot read the others. Revoking a token stops it on its next request.

roles.title: Model roles · the three names every caller uses
roles.intro: Owned by the OS. Each role below points at a model in the LiteLLM catalog. The mapping is saved as the file os/models.yml in the platform repository (versioned) and applied to LiteLLM, so os-ui, agents and apps all resolve a role the same way, at the gateway. If someone edits the alias in LiteLLM, the OS puts it back and shows it here. The catalog — the real models and their keys — is owned by LiteLLM: add or remove models there (open LiteLLM ↗).

roles.helpWorker: Assistants, agent execution and light work.

lead.title: Lead model
lead.switchLabel: Save costs: the worker model leads and the strong model is only used to escalate — lower quality and fewer capabilities.
lead.textOn: The worker model leads: it plans, chooses tools and answers, and the strong model steps in only when a check fails, the worker refuses or gives an empty answer, or the worker asks for it. Lead model now: {model}.
lead.textOff: The strong model leads: it plans, chooses tools and answers, and decides on its own which clearly defined sub-tasks go to the worker. Lead model now: {model}.
lead.trace: Every escalation is shown in the turn's model trace.

assistant.title: Assistant model · the ONE LLM behind every built-in assistant
assistant.intro: Agents & Software build chat, the Big Bets planner, the Knowledge assistant and the Metric agent all run on this one model, through the governed LiteLLM gateway. By default it follows the lead role (the strong model, unless the cost saver below is on): it plans, chooses tools and writes every answer on the lead model; the strong lead hands only clearly defined, schema-checked sub-tasks to the worker. Override it below to pin a model you added with Add a provider.
assistant.tagTitle: The model the assistant runs on right now, and the role it stands for
assistant.addHint: To use a model that is not listed, add it with Add a provider below; it then appears here.

provider.title: Add a provider · connect your own LLM backend
provider.intro: Azure OpenAI, an OpenAI-compatible server (vLLM, LM Studio, EU Router), Ollama, Mistral, STACKIT or any other provider the LiteLLM gateway supports. The connection and the model are stored in the gateway’s own database (durable across restarts); the key is kept by the gateway, encrypted, and never shown again. The provider’s host must be on the egress allowlist — if it is not, this flow says exactly what to add.

personalData.title: Governance — personal data before Company
personalData.label: Personal data before Company certification
personalData.block: Block (default) — refuse until personal data is masked or hidden
personalData.confirm: Confirm — the certifier confirms with a reason
personalData.hint: A dataset certified to Company can be read by every domain; only the masks and hides in its grants protect a column. Columns are marked as personal data in the dataset's Documentation (“Personal data: yes / no”).
personalData.detail: Block: certification is refused while a personal-data column is neither masked nor hidden; a dataset whose columns are not classified needs a classification or the certifier's confirmation that it holds no personal data. Confirm: the certifier may go ahead after ticking a confirmation and giving a reason. Off: no check. Every certification records what the rule decided (and any reason) on the dataset and in the audit log; every change to this setting is audited.

traces.title: Traces (Langfuse)
traces.mask: Mask what is sent to Langfuse
traces.pii: Personal data only (e-mail, phone, IBAN, card)
traces.content: All content (keep model, tokens, latency, cost, tool names, status)
traces.hint: Off (default) = traces are recorded as before. On = the masking happens inside os-ui, before anything is sent, and the gateway is told to leave prompts and answers out of its own record of each call. Monitoring keeps working: tokens, cost, latency, model, tool names and errors are never masked.
traces.detail: Applies without a restart or a redeploy: os-ui and the run worker read this switch on their next write (the worker within a few seconds). A run that is already in progress keeps the level it started with for its message text; personal data is masked on every export either way. Traces already stored in Langfuse are not changed. The gateway's tool definitions and ids are not message content and are not masked. Langfuse's own server-side masking is an Enterprise feature and is not used.

A refusal older than {minutes} min is raised in Monitoring and in every admin's notifications.

knowledge.label: Knowledge index
knowledge.sub: Re-chunks each workflow and domain card and re-embeds it; pasted documents are re-embedded in place.
knowledge.name: knowledge

reindex.markedVsAll: Re-index marked only finds rows that still carry evidence. Rows fabricated before the production guard carry none — a hash vector and a real vector are the same bytes in the same field — so a marked count of 0 is not a clean bill of health. Re-index everything is the only complete answer, and it spends real gateway budget.

disabled.inFlight: A batch of this re-index is running right now — it will continue on its own.
disabled.noPlan: Run Plan first — a re-index should never start before you have read what it would do.
disabled.notReady: This index cannot be re-indexed right now.
disabled.empty: Nothing selected: this filter found no unit to re-index.

abandonDisabled.inFlight: A batch is executing right now — wait for it to finish, then abandon.

reindex.alreadyRunning: A batch of this re-index is already running elsewhere; this is its progress.
reindex.abandonConfirm: Abandon this re-index? The units already replaced stay replaced; the rest are not touched, and the job is recorded as abandoned by you. You can plan and start again afterwards.
reindex.abandoned: Abandoned. The target is free to re-run.
reindex.nothingAbandoned: Nothing was running; any stale in-flight flag is cleared.

marked.label: Rows that still admit to being a stand-in
marked.help: A persisted label (source / embed_source / mode) naming a stand-in. No writer in EITHER index ever stamped one — Knowledge has a `source` field, but it holds provenance like `os-ui-ingest` — so 0 here is expected and proves nothing.

missingRepresentation.label: Units with no indexed row at all
missingRepresentation.help: A stored file or workflow the index holds nothing for — the parser produced nothing, or a refusal stopped it. Counted in UNITS, not rows: there are no rows to count.

missingVector.label: Rows with no embedding
missingVector.help: Indexed text with no vector, so it can never be found by similarity search. Pasted documents are written this way today.

dimensionMismatch.label: Rows whose dimension no longer matches
dimensionMismatch.help: The index mapping’s knn dimension differs from the configured one. OpenSearch rejects a wrong-length vector at write time, so when this is non-zero EVERY row is un-queryable.

all.label: Rows in the index
all.help: The denominator, so the other counts can be read as proportions.

estimate.text: {units, plural, other {# unit(s)}} covering {rows, plural, other {# indexed row(s)}}, in {batches, plural, other {# batch(es)}} of up to {batch}. Every selected unit is re-parsed and re-embedded through the real services, which costs real gateway budget.

reindex.confirmAll: Re-index EVERYTHING in the {target} index: {estimate} Rows that are already correct will be re-parsed and re-embedded too. Continue?
reindex.selected: {count, plural, other {# unit(s)}} selected by this scope. Index dimension {dim}, configured {configured}.
reindex.selectedCapped: {count, plural, other {# unit(s)}} selected by this scope (capped — run again afterwards for the rest). Index dimension {dim}, configured {configured}.

progress.failed: Stopped — {cursor} of {total} units, then it failed: {details}.

describeFiles.title: Describe files
describeFiles.lead: Every uploaded file gets a short description and a few tags written from its content, by one call on the standard model billed to the person who uploaded it. Restricted files and files their owner keeps stored only are never sent to a model. A description or tag a person wrote is never replaced.
describeFiles.toggle: Write a description and tags automatically for uploaded files
describeFiles.existing: Existing files. Describe the files that have text but no description or tags. Plan first: a plan writes nothing and calls no model. A run is billed to you, the admin who starts it, and works in batches you can stop; starting again only touches what is still undescribed.

runTitle.go: Describe these files, billed to you

describeFiles.confirm: Describe {count, plural, other {# file(s)}}? Each one is sent to the model once, and the calls are billed to you ({billedTo}).
describeFiles.stopped: Stopped. Plan again to continue with the rest.
describeFiles.costUnpriced: no price is set for {model}, so no cost can be estimated
describeFiles.planLine: {count, plural, other {# file(s)}} would be described with <mono>{model}</mono>. Estimate: roughly {input} input and {output} output tokens, {cost}. This is an estimate from the text lengths, not a bill.

skip.optOut: stored only by their owner’s choice
skip.described: already have a description and tags
